overview: South Australia was founded as a British settler colony in 1836 and gained its elected parliament in 1857. The map shows a late colonial slice, when farming, mining and new infrastructure transformed daily life while Aboriginal peoples faced dispossession.

periods.title: Settlement on Aboriginal lands
periods.summary: Colonial settlement expanded across existing Indigenous homelands, with farming and mining driving growth.

periods.title: Parliament, engineering and reform
periods.summary: An elected parliament governed the colony, which also administered the Northern Territory before federation.

sections.title: A colony built on contested land

items.text: South Australia recruited free settlers rather than receiving transported convicts to construct its public works. Farms grew wheat and grapes, pastoralists raised livestock, and copper mines attracted workers. These opportunities for newcomers accompanied the loss of Aboriginal land and deaths from introduced disease.

The 1836 Letters Patent included a protection for Aboriginal people’s occupation and enjoyment of their lands. Reading that promise beside the history of dispossession reveals a central contradiction of the colonial project: words on official parchment did not ensure protection in practice.

At Burra, miners and their families dug homes into creek banks because conventional housing was scarce and costly. Some dwellings had several rooms. Flooding in 1851 devastated this improvised neighbourhood; most dugout homes were abandoned by about 1860.

Burra’s copper industry imported Cornish steam engines, hauled inland on purpose-built bullock wagons. Smelting also drew workers from Germany and mule drivers from Chile. A mining town in South Australia was connected to people and machinery on several continents.

In 1877, Adelaide had thousands of cesspits beneath the city, while raw sewage also reached the River Torrens. Toilets created a city-sized problem long before every household could simply flush and forget. New drainage was an important public-health investment.

The underground sewerage system was completed in 1881. Waste went to a sewage farm near Islington, where land treatment was part of the disposal system. By 1885 it handled almost two million gallons daily: an impressive amount of unglamorous engineering.

The Education Act of 1875 made school attendance compulsory on a part-time basis. That qualification matters: the new rule was a step towards public schooling, rather than today’s full school timetable arriving everywhere overnight.

Completed in 1872, the Overland Telegraph linked Adelaide and Darwin. Connection to the submarine cable then shortened communication with Europe from months to hours. Messages travelled electrically, but maintaining the long line still required workers, supplies and difficult journeys.

The line used about 36,000 poles and eleven repeater stations to refresh the signal. Its route drew upon Aboriginal travel routes and water knowledge. Those stations also became starting points for further settler expansion into the interior.

Charles Todd’s 1872 announcement includes the English words “a line of communications two thousand miles long.” In everyday modern terms, he meant a messaging connection about 3,200 kilometres long. The museum reproduces this contemporary wording: an engineer announcing that the wires finally joined.

The 1894 women’s suffrage petition carried more than 11,600 names. Its sheets were glued together, rolled up and tied with a gold ribbon. Organizing votes for women involved thousands of conversations and signatures, not just one dramatic parliamentary speech.

Parliament passed the suffrage bill in December 1894; royal assent followed in February 1895. Women, including Aboriginal women, gained eligibility both to vote and to stand for parliament. The achievement came after repeated failed attempts and persistent campaigning.

ending.text: On 1 January 1901, South Australia became a state of the Commonwealth of Australia. Federation divided powers between state and federal governments; it did not end the community or erase its parliament. The map’s 1900 endpoint marks the approach to that transition.
